generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the cycle runs across a whole module in the School of Sport and beyond it. What you learn about training theory and testing shapes how you approach the programme design, the design produces feedback, and the feedback, once you use it, changes how you plan and prescribe the next block. Seeing a single programme as one turn of that cycle, rather than a one-off, is what lets each piece of work build on the last instead of starting from scratch, which matters most when you reach your independent project.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two strength and conditioning students finish a module with the same comment on their final programme design: a solid summary of the training principles, but you needed to take more of an analytical position of your own.

Tom treats learning, assessment and feedback as three things that happen and then end. The module is over and the mark is in, so he reads the comment once and files it away. Nothing about it changes how he approaches the next module, and when the next programme comes back the same comment is there again: the cycle has simply repeated.

Amara treats the same comment as the start of the next round rather than the end of this one. It becomes something to act on: she plans the next programme around taking a clear analytical position, and carries that into how she reads the training evidence and designs the block from the outset. The next piece takes a position, and it is stronger, because the feedback fed back into the learning.

Both got the same comment. Only Amara treated the three as one cycle, letting feedback feed the next round of learning. That is what connects them, and it is what turns each programme into the start of the next improvement rather than a repeat of the last.
generatedProse.summary: Learning, assessment and feedback are easiest to deal with one at a time, but in the School of Sport they work as one connected cycle, where each part feeds the next and the whole comes round again. You can now show how they connect rather than stand alone, and recognise that cycle in your own experience of a module. Seeing the loop is what lets you carry effort from one part into the others, so that each programme becomes the start of the next improvement, right through to your independent project.

check.body: A strength and conditioning student does well in one programme design, reads the feedback, and uses it to plan the next programme, which comes back stronger. Which part of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle did using that feedback feed back into?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following programme improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first programme, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next programme.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following programme improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next programme, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next programme improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.
